To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) collectively owned water supply schemes in rural South Africa have emerged as a result of the failure of the state to deliver services; 2) the schemes have been constructed, operated and maintained by the communities; 3) they are characterized by a high degree of community participation and ownership; 4) the schemes are generally well functioning, reliable and of high quality; 5) they are characterized as being sustainable in terms of operation and maintenance, but not in terms of resource access;

(i) the emergence and performance of self supply water schemes are influenced by a variety of factors, (ii) self supply water schemes can be an important source of learning for public service delivery, (iii) the performance of self supply schemes can be improved by learning from their own experiences, and (iv) the performance of public service delivery can be improved by taking self supply schemes into account in policy and planning.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How can the state and communities learn from each other?
the question how we can learn from these schemes and how we can improve the public provision of services in rural South Africa.
the question of how to improve public approaches and service delivery by studying and learning from rural self supply initiatives.

the cases of Tshakhuma show the potential of self supply, but also its limitations, which need to be carefully considered when considering its role in public service delivery in South Africa.

self supply systems are a complex and dynamic phenomenon, that is not easy to describe and assess.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the cases described in this article show the potential of self supply as an important alternative to public water supply, but that this potential needs to be harnessed through a more enabling environment and a better understanding of self supply.

we need to better understand the dynamics of rural self supply and how it interacts with the state, and that we should consider how the state can learn from and engage with rural self supply initiatives.
self supply schemes can be a useful complement to public service delivery.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we need a more nuanced understanding of the potential and limitations of self supply in order to better inform policy and practice in the field of public service delivery.
we should recognize and study such initiatives as prototypes for service delivery.
self supply is a viable alternative to public water supply, but that the sustainability of these schemes depends on the extent to which they are integrated with public service delivery.
